scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Ciranda originates from the northeastern region of Brazil, specifically across Paraíba and Pernambuco, with deep historical ties to Ilha de Itamaracá.
Its roots trace back to Portugal, before it heavily popularized in Pernambuco during the 1960s and 1970s as an evolution or successor to the coco dance.
Folklore credits the dance's inception to the wives of local fishermen who sang and danced on the sand while awaiting the return of fishing boats from the sea.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Ciranda functions as an egalitarian community ritual and celebratory gathering free of social, racial, or economic prejudice.
It serves as a vital cultural anchor during local festivals and public celebrations across the Brazilian northeast, uniting generations in continuous circular motion.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers form a large open or closed circle, holding hands and facing the center while moving clockwise.
Marking the heavy bass stroke of the zabumba, dancers stamp firmly with the left foot forward, executing two steps backward and two steps forward.
The dance is fully communal with no limits on participants; individuals may enter or leave the ring freely.
Watch for Left-foot stamp and step sequence.

Formation: large ring on beaches and squares, moving to the right, inner ring forms if too large

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The musical accompaniment follows a slow, simple quaternary rhythm dominated by percussion.
The primary beat is marked by a deep, resonant stroke of the zabumba (or bumbo) on the head of the measure, combined with muffled strokes on other beats.
Listen for the zabumba, tarol, ganzá, maracá.
The pulse is quaternário simples.

A slow, unhurried quaternary pulse driven by the heavy bass thud of the zabumba on beat one, surrounded by the dry rattle of the ganzá and maracá, while a lead singer carries a repetitive, call-and-response refrain.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Traditionally performed outdoors in public squares and along sandy ocean beaches, particularly in coastal northeastern Brazil.
Participants wear everyday clothing suited for community gatherings, as the dance is open to all socioeconomic backgrounds without formal costume requirements.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Prominent traditional masters and exponents of ciranda include Lia de Itamaracá, Penha Cirandeira, Odete de Pilar, Mestre Baracho, Tina, Dona Edite, Cida, Vó Mera, Mestre Cícero, Mestre Mané Baixinho, and Mestre Anderson Miguel.
Ciranda is primarily anchored across the states of Pernambuco and Paraíba, sharing close historical and stylistic lineage with the regional coco dance forms of northeastern Brazil.
Derived from Portuguese roots blended with regional northeastern Brazilian traditions, ciranda evolved in proximity to and outnumbering the traditional coco dance during the mid-20th century.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Ciranda is variant of Coco: Ciranda absorbed influences from and supplanted the older coco dance style in Pernambuco.
Ciranda is shares music of Quadrilha: Both are prominent traditional festive dance forms of northeastern Brazil.

Rhythm pattern: toque grave da zabumba na cabeça do compasso e toques abafados nos outros tempos. Instruments: zabumba, tarol, ganzá, maracá, pandeiro, cuíca, accordion. Vocal style: entoada pelo mestre cirandeiro with simple melodies and refrains. Mood: slow, community, repeated, celebratory. It should sound like this: A slow, unhurried quaternary pulse driven by the heavy bass thud of the zabumba on beat one, surrounded by the dry rattle of the ganzá and maracá, while a lead singer carries a repetitive, call-and-response refrain.
